title: WHY DID GOD ALLOW POLYGAMY FOR CENTURIES?
paragraphs:
WHY DID GOD ALLOW POLYGAMY FOR CENTURIES?
The Bible records Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon having multiple wives. So was God approving it—or was Scripture showing us something far more devastating about the human heart?
There is a question many Christians quietly hope nobody asks.
Because once someone asks it, the easy answers begin falling apart.
“If marriage is supposed to be between one man and one woman, why did God allow men in the Bible to have multiple wives?”
Abraham.
Jacob.
David.
Solomon.
These are not obscure villains hidden in forgotten genealogies.
They are some of the most recognizable names in Scripture.
And some of them had more than one wife.
So what are we supposed to do with that?
Pretend those passages are not there?
Explain them away?
Say, “Well, that was the Old Testament,” and quickly change the subject?
No.
The Bible does not need us to protect it from difficult questions.
It needs us to read it carefully enough to hear what it is actually saying.
Because one of the greatest mistakes we can make when reading Scripture is assuming that everything the Bible describes is something God prescribes.
The Bible records murder.
It does not endorse murder.
It records adultery.
It does not endorse adultery.
It records deception, incest, betrayal, drunkenness, idolatry, slavery, violence, political corruption, family dysfunction, and catastrophic moral failure.
Why?
Because the Bible is not propaganda for humanity.
It is the story of God entering humanity's wreckage to redeem it.
And that changes the question.
Maybe we should not merely ask:
“Why did God allow polygamy?”
Maybe we should also ask:
“What happened when human beings departed from God's original design?”
Because the first marriage in Scripture does not begin with a king surrounded by wives.
It begins in a garden.
Before Abraham.
Before Jacob.
Before David.
Before Solomon.
Before Moses.
Before Israel.
Before sin had shattered human relationships.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
And there was God.
Genesis 2:24 says in Hebrew:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
‘Al-kēn ya‘ăzov-’ish ’et-’aviv ve’et-’immo, vedavaq be’ishto, vehayu levasar echad.
Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother, clings to his wife, and they become one flesh.
The words matter.
וְדָבַק — vedavaq.
He clings. He cleaves. He holds fast.
And then:
בָשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
One flesh.
Not merely a contract.
Not merely sexual access.
Not merely reproduction.
A covenantal union in which two lives become joined.
This is where the biblical story of marriage begins.
And centuries later, when religious leaders tried to drag Jesus into an argument about what Moses permitted, Jesus did something extraordinary.
He went backward.
Past Moses.
Past Israel's legislation.
Past centuries of broken human history.
Back to creation.
Jesus pointed to God's intention “from the beginning.”
That distinction matters enormously.
Because Scripture sometimes shows God dealing with human beings not as humanity ought to be, but as fallen humanity actually is.
Jesus gives us one of the clearest examples when discussing divorce.
The Greek of Matthew 19:8 reads:
λέγει αὐτοῖς ὅτι Μωϋσῆς πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν ἐπέτρεψεν ὑμῖν ἀπολῦσαι τὰς γυναῖκας ὑμῶν, ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δὲ οὐ γέγονεν οὕτως.
The crucial word is:
σκληροκαρδίαν — sklērokardian.
Hardness of heart.
Jesus says Moses permitted divorce because of their hardness of heart, then immediately says:
ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δὲ οὐ γέγονεν οὕτως
ap’ archēs de ou gegonen houtōs.
“But from the beginning it was not so.”
Notice what Jesus is doing.
Permission within a fallen society is not automatically identical to God's original ideal.
That verse is specifically about divorce, not polygamy, so we should not put words into Jesus' mouth and claim He was directly explaining every Old Testament plural marriage.
But the principle He reveals is extremely important.
God can regulate human brokenness without declaring that brokenness beautiful.
And suddenly, much of the Old Testament begins to make more sense.
When polygamy first explicitly appears in the biblical narrative, it does not appear in Eden.
It appears in Genesis 4.
And the man associated with it is Lamech.
“And Lamech took unto him two wives.”
That sentence is more significant than it first appears.
Lamech belongs to Cain's line, and the narrative soon presents him boasting about violence and vengeance.
The Bible does not introduce polygamy by saying, “And God commanded Lamech to take another wife.”
It simply tells us what Lamech did.
Humanity has left Eden.
Sin is spreading.
Violence is escalating.
Relationships are fracturing.
And now the marriage pattern of Genesis 2 has also been disrupted.
Then the pattern continues through history.
Abraham has Sarah and Hagar, and what follows?
Pain.
Jealousy.
Humiliation.
Conflict.
A woman fleeing into the wilderness.
A household torn apart.
Jacob ends up with Leah and Rachel.
What follows?
Rivalry.
Tears.
Competition.
A woman desperately longing to be loved.
Sisters measuring their worth against one another through children.
Read those chapters slowly enough and they stop feeling like ancient genealogy.
They begin feeling like a wounded family sitting around your dinner table.
Leah knows what it feels like to lie beside someone whose heart belongs somewhere else.
Rachel knows what it feels like to look at another woman's children while carrying an ache she cannot fix.
Jacob's household becomes a battlefield of longing, favoritism, jealousy, fertility, rejection, and competition.
The Bible never has to insert a sentence saying, “Polygamy causes complications.”
It shows you the complications.
That is one of Scripture's most powerful teaching methods.
Sometimes God gives you a command.
Sometimes He gives you a consequence.
David's household becomes even darker.
His multiplication of wives exists alongside a royal family increasingly marked by sexual sin, rivalry, betrayal, violence, and bloodshed.
Then comes Solomon.
The king who had almost everything.
Wisdom.
Wealth.
Power.
Prestige.
Influence.
And women.
Many women.
But centuries before Solomon was born, Deuteronomy had already warned Israel's future king not to multiply wives for himself lest his heart turn away.
The warning was there.
The boundary was there.
And Solomon crossed it spectacularly.
His marriages became entangled with the turning of his heart toward other gods.
So the Bible is not hiding the wreckage.
It is displaying it.
That matters because people sometimes reason like this:
“David had multiple wives, therefore God approved of multiple wives.”
But that logic would force us to approve everything else David did simply because Scripture records him doing it.
David committed adultery.
David arranged Uriah's death.
Scripture records those acts with brutal honesty precisely because biblical heroes are not the Savior.
That title belongs to Someone else.
The Bible is filled with deeply flawed men because the Bible is not ultimately about the greatness of men.
It is about the faithfulness of God.
Abraham cannot carry the story.
Jacob cannot carry it.
Moses cannot carry it.
David cannot carry it.
Solomon cannot carry it.
Every human hero eventually develops cracks.
And through those cracks Scripture keeps whispering:
You need Someone better.
This is where the question becomes personal.
Because perhaps you have never practiced polygamy.
But you know what it means to ask God to tolerate something He never called good.
We all know how to do that.
“God understands.”
“Everybody does it.”
“It isn't hurting anyone.”
“This is just how life works now.”
“Surely God won't mind.”
We become remarkably sophisticated theologians when we are defending the thing we do not want to surrender.
And this is where the ancient question about polygamy stops being an argument about ancient Near Eastern households and becomes a mirror.
Because the deeper story is about the terrifying patience of God with sinners.
Why didn't God destroy Jacob the moment his family became dysfunctional?
Why didn't He abandon David?
Why didn't He erase Israel every time they wandered?
Why did He continue working through people whose lives were painfully inconsistent with His holiness?
Because patience is not approval.
Mercy is not endorsement.
And God's willingness to work through broken people does not mean He celebrates their brokenness.
If it did, none of us would have hope.
Think about that.
If God only worked through people whose lives already perfectly reflected His design, Scripture would be very short.
And your story and mine would never make it past the first page.
God meets people in the wreckage.
But He does not call the wreckage Eden.
That distinction is everything.
The Old Testament law itself sometimes regulates situations it does not present as creation's ideal.
There are laws dealing with households where a man has two wives. Those laws protect rights and restrict injustice within realities already present in Israelite society.
Regulation is not necessarily celebration.
A guardrail beside a dangerous road is not an advertisement for driving off the cliff.
It exists because the danger is real.
And God repeatedly acts in Scripture to restrain the damage human sin does to other human beings.
This is why Deuteronomy 17:17 becomes so important.
Israel's king was warned not to “multiply wives” for himself so that his heart would not turn away.
God was not giving kings an unlimited divine endorsement of royal harems.
The Torah itself placed a warning directly against their multiplication.
And the biblical history eventually shows exactly why.
Solomon becomes the living cautionary tale.
But there is another witness people often overlook.
Malachi describes the wife as a covenant companion and confronts men for faithlessness toward “the wife of your youth.”
Marriage is not treated casually.
It is covenant.
And when Jesus arrives, He does not announce a revolutionary definition invented in first-century Galilee.
He reaches back to Genesis.
The beginning.
The garden.
The one-flesh union.
Then the New Testament continues with language such as Paul's requirement that an overseer be:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα
mias gynaikos andra.
Literally, an expression meaning a “one-woman man,” traditionally rendered “the husband of one wife.”
Christ does not move God's people farther from covenant faithfulness.
He calls them deeper into it.
But even that is not the deepest point.
Because Christian marriage ultimately points beyond marriage.
Paul says in Ephesians 5 that the mystery points to Christ and the Church.
And now everything changes.
Jesus does not collect disposable brides.
He has a Bride.
He does not exploit her.
He gives Himself for her.
He does not use covenant for His convenience.
He sheds His blood to establish covenant.
He does not abandon His Bride when she becomes difficult to love.
He sanctifies her.
Cleanses her.
Keeps her.
Loves her.
The ultimate answer to humanity's distorted love is not merely better marriage legislation.
It is Jesus Christ.
Because sin always takes what God made beautiful and bends it inward toward ourselves.
Love becomes possession.
Leadership becomes domination.
Sex becomes consumption.
Marriage becomes convenience.
Power becomes entitlement.
And religion itself can become camouflage.
But then Jesus walks into the wreckage.
Not to pretend the wreckage is beautiful.
To redeem the people trapped inside it.
That is the Gospel.
Christ does not stand at the edge of our scandals shouting instructions about how to climb out.
He enters our world.
He touches lepers.
He eats with sinners.
He speaks with the sexually broken.
He confronts hypocrites.
He welcomes repentant people.
He carries a cross.
And on that cross, the sinless Bridegroom dies for an unfaithful people.
That is why grace must never be confused with permission.
Grace is not God saying:
“Your sin doesn't matter.”
Grace is God saying:
“Your sin mattered enough that My Son bled for it—and I love you enough not to leave you enslaved to it.”
Maybe that is the sentence someone reading this needed.
Because perhaps your scandal has nothing to do with multiple wives.
Maybe it is pornography nobody knows about.
Maybe it is adultery you have carefully hidden.
Maybe it is emotional infidelity you keep calling “just friendship.”
Maybe it is bitterness toward your spouse.
Maybe your marriage is collapsing quietly while your Facebook photographs still look perfect.
Maybe you have been betrayed.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Maybe you are divorced and carrying shame you cannot seem to put down.
Maybe you grew up inside a home where “marriage” meant screaming, fear, manipulation, abandonment, or violence.
Maybe the word “family” does not make you feel safe.
Maybe it makes your chest tighten.
Hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that brokenness was never broken.
The Gospel is the announcement that brokenness does not have to have the final word.
Jesus does.
That is why our message will always be:
Not from scandal to denial.
Not from scandal to excuses.
Not from scandal to religious pretending.
From scandal...
to repentance.
From scandal...
to forgiveness.
From scandal...
to restoration.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He does not rewrite history by pretending it never happened.
He rewrites what history gets to become in the hands of a redeemed person.
Peter still denied Him.
But denial did not write Peter's final chapter.
Paul still persecuted Christians.
But persecution did not write Paul's final chapter.
The woman caught in adultery really had a scandal.
The Samaritan woman's relational history was real.
The thief really was dying beside Jesus for crimes he had committed.
The Gospel does not require fake backstories.
It creates redeemed endings.
And perhaps that is why the uncomfortable marriages of the Old Testament were never edited out.
We need to see them.
We need to see Abraham's household hurting.
We need to hear Leah crying.
We need to watch David's family fracture.
We need to see Solomon surrounded by abundance while his heart wanders.
Because Scripture is showing us again and again:
Having more does not heal the heart.
More women could not satisfy Solomon.
More power could not satisfy David.
More children could not make Leah feel fully loved by Jacob.
More human affection cannot fill the place designed for God.
And thousands of years later, we are still doing the same thing.
More followers.
More money.
More attention.
More relationships.
More sexual experiences.
More purchases.
More achievements.
More validation.
More.
More.
More.
And still...
the heart aches.
Perhaps the real scandal is not simply that ancient men accumulated wives.
Perhaps the scandal is that humanity keeps trying to multiply created things until they become enough to replace the Creator.
They never do.
Only Christ is enough.
So why did God allow polygamy to continue for centuries?
Scripture does not give us one isolated verse saying, “Here is the complete philosophical explanation for why I tolerated every plural marriage in biblical history.”
We should be humble enough to admit that.
But Scripture gives us enough to see the pattern.
God's creation establishes the one-flesh marriage union.
Human sin distorts what God made.
Biblical narrative honestly records that distortion.
The law restrains injustice within a fallen society and specifically warns kings against multiplying wives.
The narratives repeatedly expose the suffering surrounding plural marriages.
The prophets call God's people toward covenant faithfulness.
Jesus points back to what was true “from the beginning.”
And the New Testament ultimately reveals marriage as a sign pointing toward Christ and His Bride.
The Bible's trajectory is not from monogamy toward increasingly celebrated polygamy.
It points back toward covenant fidelity.
Back toward the beginning.
And ultimately forward toward the Bridegroom.
Jesus.
Maybe you started reading because you wanted an answer about polygamy.
But perhaps the Holy Spirit has brought you somewhere more uncomfortable.
Your own heart.
Because it is easy to put Solomon on trial.
Harder to ask what we have multiplied until it began stealing our hearts from God.
It is easy to analyze Jacob's dysfunctional home.
Harder to confront what we keep tolerating in ours.
It is easy to debate David's failures.
Harder to confess our own.
So don't leave this article merely knowing more.
Ask the question that matters:
“Jesus, what have I been asking You to tolerate that You are asking me to surrender?”
Stay there for a moment.
No performance.
No church language.
No pretending.
Just you and Christ.
If something came to mind...
don't run from it.
Run to Him.
Repentance is not the doorway into humiliation.
For the person who comes to Christ, repentance is the doorway home.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That is 1 John 1:9.
Not “some unrighteousness.”
Not “everything except the thing you're ashamed to name.”
All.
The blood of Jesus is stronger than the chapter you wish you could erase.
So if this exposed something hidden in you, you do not need to explain the details publicly. But you can make a simple declaration of surrender.
Let other believers know they are not the only ones fighting.
It does not.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift in Christ.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping biblical teaching reach people who desperately need it.

Invite your family. Invite the friend who has drifted. Invite the believer who is barely holding on. Invite the skeptic with hard questions. Even invite the person who thinks Christianity has nothing left to say to them.
There is only one Savior.
There is only one cross.
There is only one blood sufficient to cleanse sin.
Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is the most beautiful answer hidden inside this uncomfortable question.
The Bible does not hide the scandals of its people because God was never building His story around flawless human beings.
He was leading us toward a flawless Savior.
Abraham failed.
Jacob failed.
David failed.
Solomon failed.
Israel failed.
We fail.
But Jesus Christ remained faithful.
And when our sin multiplied, grace did not become permission to remain unchanged.
Grace came looking for us...
to forgive us,
to transform us,
and to bring us home.
God may meet you in the ruins, but He loves you too much to let the ruins become the name of your final chapter.
